{\LARGE\bfseries\sffamily\color{AtlasNavy} Finite-sum minimization with possibly nonconvex components: strongly convex average and mean-square component smoothness; selected component gradients\par}\vspace{5pt}
\textbf{Setting ID.} \texttt{SO\_\allowbreak{}\allowbreak{}FO\_\allowbreak{}\allowbreak{}F02\_\allowbreak{}\allowbreak{}sc\_\allowbreak{}\allowbreak{}ms}

Single-objective optimization

Find an approximate global minimizer, with accuracy measured by suboptimality of the complete objective.

\textbf{Status.} Bounds missing

\textbf{TASK tags.} formulation: Global minimization; task family: Single objective

\textbf{MODEL tags.} convexity: Possibly nonconvex components; convexity: Strongly convex; geometry: Full space; smoothness: Lipschitz gradient; smoothness: Mean square smooth components; structure: Finite sum

\textbf{ORACLE tags.} access order: First-order interface; feedback quality: Exact; interface family: Component gradient; operation: Component gradient; public information: Hidden objects explicitly declared; public information: Known lower bound; public information: Known upper bound; public information: Known exact value; public information: Public inputs explicitly declared

\textbf{ALGORITHMS tags.} adaptivity: Adaptive; adaptivity: Explicit restriction; computation: Internal arithmetic uncharged; randomization: Deterministic algorithms; randomization: Private randomness allowed; restriction: Linear span; restriction: No additional span restriction explicitly imposed

\needspace{7\baselineskip}\section{1. Setting specification}
\needspace{4\baselineskip}\subsection{Task}
Find an approximate global minimizer, with accuracy measured by suboptimality of the complete objective.


\AtlasMath{\min_{x\in \mathbb{R}^d}F(x)}


The complete objective is the finite sum \AtlasInlineMath{F(x)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n f_i(x)}. Component information is available only through the declared component oracle.

\needspace{4\baselineskip}\subsection{Admissible model}
\AtlasInlineMath{F=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n f_i}, where the components may be nonconvex. The average \AtlasInlineMath{F} is globally \AtlasInlineMath{\mu}-strongly convex and has initial suboptimality at most \AtlasInlineMath{\Delta}. The components are mean-square smooth: \AtlasInlineMath{\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\|\nabla f_i(x)-\nabla f_i(y)\|_2^2\le\beta^2\|x-y\|_2^2}.

Unless another geometry is specified, vectors use the Euclidean norm \AtlasInlineMath{\|\cdot\|_2}, and matrices and higher derivatives use the corresponding operator norm. The assumptions hold uniformly throughout the declared domain.

Admissible parameter domain:


\AtlasMath{\begin{gathered}\varepsilon > 0,\quad d \ge 1,\quad n \ge 1,\quad \mu > 0\\\kappa \ge 1,\quad \varepsilon \le c\,\Delta,\quad \beta > 0,\quad \Delta > 0\\\mu \le \beta\end{gathered}}


\needspace{4\baselineskip}\subsection{Oracle interface}
Public numerical inputs: \AtlasInlineMath{d,\ n,\ \varepsilon}.

Public upper bounds: \AtlasInlineMath{\beta,\ \Delta}.

Public lower bounds: \AtlasInlineMath{\mu}.

The unknown objects are the component functions \AtlasInlineMath{f_1,\ldots,f_n}.

For each query, the algorithm chooses \AtlasInlineMath{i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}} and \AtlasInlineMath{x\in\mathbb R^d} and receives the following information about that component.


\AtlasMath{\nabla f_i(x)}


All responses come from one fixed unknown instance. The algorithm adaptively chooses query points and any indices permitted by the interface.

\needspace{4\baselineskip}\subsection{Output}
Return a point \AtlasInlineMath{\widehat x\in\mathbb R^d}.

The output may be unqueried or constructed from the query history, provided it is feasible. No additional function value or accuracy certificate is required.

\needspace{4\baselineskip}\subsection{Loss or accuracy criterion}

\AtlasMath{\ell(I,\widehat{x})=F(\widehat{x})-F^\star}


\AtlasInlineMath{F^\star=\inf_{x\in \mathbb{R}^d}F(x)}. The existence, compactness, or initial-suboptimality assumptions ensure that the optimal value in this comparison is finite.

\needspace{4\baselineskip}\subsection{Resource accounting}
One selected-component gradient costs one call; a two-point difference costs two, and a full gradient costs \AtlasInlineMath{n}.

Real arithmetic, precision, and storage applied to already available information are uncharged. Public geometric operations are limited to those explicitly granted by the oracle. Query complexity alone does not imply arithmetic, memory, or communication complexity.

\needspace{4\baselineskip}\subsection{Algorithm views and success guarantees}
\needspace{4\baselineskip}\subsubsection{Randomized / Expected loss}
Private randomization is allowed. Queries, stopping decisions, and postprocessing may adapt to observed feedback.

No additional span, zero-respecting, linear-iteration, or memory restriction is imposed.

Interaction is adaptive to the feedback history. Every actual response is charged separately, including responses in parallel or batch queries. Internal real arithmetic, storage, and postprocessing are uncharged.

Select an algorithm using the public parameters, and then require the following for every admissible instance and response rule:


\AtlasMath{\forall I\,\forall\mathcal{O}\in\mathcal{O}(I):\ \mathbb{E}_{A,\mathcal{O}}\ell(I,\widehat{x})\le\varepsilon}


The probability space includes the algorithm's private randomness. The instance and its admissible oracle law are fixed before randomness is averaged.

\textbf{Resource qualification.} Cost is bounded in expectation for every instance: \AtlasInlineMath{\sup_{I,\mathcal O}\mathbb E N_A\le T}. This contract is not replaced by a fixed bound on every execution path.

\needspace{4\baselineskip}\subsubsection{Randomized / Linear span / Expected loss}
Private randomization is allowed. Queries, stopping decisions, and postprocessing may adapt to observed feedback.

Queries and outputs belong to the permitted span of historical gradients. Randomized index selection is allowed.

Interaction is adaptive to the feedback history. Every actual response is charged separately, including responses in parallel or batch queries. Internal real arithmetic, storage, and postprocessing are uncharged.

Select an algorithm using the public parameters, and then require the following for every admissible instance and response rule:


\AtlasMath{\forall I\,\forall\mathcal{O}\in\mathcal{O}(I):\ \mathbb{E}_{A,\mathcal{O}}\ell(I,\widehat{x})\le\varepsilon}


The probability space includes the algorithm's private randomness. The instance and its admissible oracle law are fixed before randomness is averaged.

\textbf{Output qualification.} The output must also satisfy the support, atomic-hull, or historical-span restriction of its algorithm view. An unqueried output remains subject to these restrictions.

\textbf{Resource qualification.} Cost is bounded in expectation for every instance: \AtlasInlineMath{\sup_{I,\mathcal O}\mathbb E N_A\le T}. This contract is not replaced by a fixed bound on every execution path.

\needspace{4\baselineskip}\subsubsection{Deterministic / Pointwise guarantee}
The algorithm uses no private random numbers. Query and stopping decisions may depend adaptively on the observed feedback.

No additional span, zero-respecting, linear-iteration, or memory restriction is imposed.

Interaction is adaptive to the feedback history. Every actual response is charged separately, including responses in parallel or batch queries. Internal real arithmetic, storage, and postprocessing are uncharged.

Select an algorithm using the public parameters, and then require the following for every admissible instance and response rule:


\AtlasMath{\forall I\,\forall\mathcal{O}\in\mathcal{O}(I):\ \ell(I,\widehat{x})\le\varepsilon}


The error guarantee holds for every instance; it is not averaged over an input distribution.

\textbf{Resource qualification.} Cost is bounded uniformly on every execution path. All calls used for initialization, repetition, batching, or candidate verification are counted.

\needspace{7\baselineskip}\section{2. Notation and parameters}
\AtlasInlineMath{x,\widehat{x}}: Query points and final output; their permitted spaces are specified separately by the oracle and output contracts \textbf{Domain:} \AtlasInlineMath{\widehat{x}\in \mathbb{R}^d}.

\AtlasInlineMath{f_i,F}: Unknown components and finite-sum objective \textbf{Domain:} \AtlasInlineMath{i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}}.


\AtlasMath{F(x)=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n f_i(x)}


\AtlasInlineMath{\nabla f_i}: Full gradient of differentiable component \AtlasInlineMath{i}

\AtlasInlineMath{F^\star}: Optimal value of the complete task; the oracle need not return it


\AtlasMath{F^\star=\inf_{x\in \mathbb{R}^d}F(x)}


\AtlasInlineMath{\mathbb{R}^d}: Real vector space with \AtlasInlineMath{d} coordinates

\AtlasInlineMath{\|\cdot\|_2,\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle}: Euclidean norm and inner product

\AtlasInlineMath{d}: Ambient dimension; a positive integer tracked explicitly. \textbf{Domain:} \AtlasInlineMath{d\in\mathbb{N}_{\ge1}}.

\AtlasInlineMath{n}: Public number of components in the finite sum or finite maximum. \textbf{Domain:} \AtlasInlineMath{n\in\mathbb{N}_{\ge1}}.

\AtlasInlineMath{\beta}: Public upper bound on the gradient smoothness constant. Any mean-square interpretation is specified in the model. \textbf{Domain:} \AtlasInlineMath{\beta>0}.

\AtlasInlineMath{\mu}: Lower bound on the strong-convexity modulus of the objective specified by the model \textbf{Domain:} \AtlasInlineMath{\mu>0}.

\AtlasInlineMath{R}: Upper bound on the distance from the public initial point to a minimizer \textbf{Domain:} \AtlasInlineMath{R>0}.

\AtlasInlineMath{\Delta}: Public upper bound on initial suboptimality. \textbf{Domain:} \AtlasInlineMath{\Delta>0}.

\AtlasInlineMath{\varepsilon}: Target tolerance for the underlying error defined by the accuracy measure \textbf{Domain:} \AtlasInlineMath{\varepsilon>0}.

\AtlasInlineMath{c}: Sufficiently small universal positive constant, potentially different between theorems; it is not a numerical threshold. \textbf{Domain:} \AtlasInlineMath{0<c<1}.

\AtlasInlineMath{C}: Sufficiently large universal constant, independent of the tracked parameters; no numerical value is specified. \textbf{Domain:} \AtlasInlineMath{C>1}.

\AtlasInlineMath{\kappa}: \AtlasInlineMath{\beta/\mu}.


\AtlasMath{\kappa=\frac{\beta}{\mu}}


\AtlasInlineMath{d_{\rm dense}}: Sufficient finite dimension for Dense Weak Hiding v3. The theorem takes the worst case over finite dimensions; it does not hold for every prescribed \AtlasInlineMath{d}. \textbf{Domain:} \AtlasInlineMath{d_{\rm dense}(n,\kappa,\Delta/\varepsilon)}.

\AtlasInlineMath{T}: Total budget for the declared resource projection; for a risk curve, the budget is fixed in advance \textbf{Domain:} \AtlasInlineMath{T\in\mathbb{N}_{\ge0}}.

\AtlasInlineMath{\ell}: The underlying loss or error defined by the accuracy measure; its expected, probabilistic, or worst-case aggregation is specified by the success contract

\AtlasInlineMath{I,\mathcal{O},A}: Admissible instance, a response rule consistent with that instance, and an algorithm; the algorithm is selected before the unknown instance

\AtlasInlineMath{\mathbb{E}}: Expectation over the declared randomness after fixing the instance and admissible response law

\AtlasInlineMath{O,\Omega,\Theta,\widetilde{O},\widetilde\Omega}: Notation for asymptotic upper and lower bounds, constant-factor matching rates, and explicitly permitted logarithmic factors. Hidden-constant dependence is specified in each regime.

\AtlasInlineMath{\log}: Natural logarithm; changing to another fixed base affects only a constant

\AtlasInlineMath{d_{\rm ZG}}: Sufficient dimension for the Zhou-Gu (2019), Theorem 4.1/4.2, lower-bound construction, chosen for the specified accuracy and parameters. This is not a fixed-low-dimensional conclusion. \textbf{Domain:} \AtlasInlineMath{d_{\rm ZG}=d_{\rm ZG}(n,\beta,\mu,R,\Delta,\varepsilon)}.

\begingroup\raggedright\sloppy A full gradient of \$F=\allowbreak{}n\textasciicircum{}\{-1\}\textbackslash{}sum\_\allowbreak{}i f\_\allowbreak{}i\$ costs \$n\$ component calls. Mean-square smoothness implies\newline{}\$\$\newline{}\textbackslash{}|\textbackslash{}nabla F(x)-\textbackslash{}nabla F(y)\textbackslash{}|\newline{}\textbackslash{}le(n\textasciicircum{}\{-1\}\textbackslash{}sum\_\allowbreak{}i\textbackslash{}|\textbackslash{}nabla f\_\allowbreak{}i(x)-\textbackslash{}nabla f\_\allowbreak{}i(y)\textbackslash{}|\textasciicircum{}2)\textasciicircum{}\{1/\allowbreak{}2\}\newline{}\textbackslash{}le\textbackslash{}beta\textbackslash{}|x-y\textbackslash{}|.\newline{}\$\$\newline{}Individual smoothness also implies this. Full-gradient convex,\allowbreak{} strongly convex,\allowbreak{} PL,\allowbreak{} stationarity,\allowbreak{} and certificate algorithms therefore transfer with an \$n\$ multiplier. A zero-query endpoint remains zero. Convexity or PL of the average must be stated separately.\newline{}\newline{}For an unrestricted smooth finite-sum \$\textbackslash{}Omega(n)\$ baseline,\allowbreak{} hide an index \$J\$. All components have public quadratic curvature \$\textbackslash{}beta\$;\allowbreak{} only component \$J\$ has an unknown linear term \$\textbackslash{}mp n\textbackslash{}beta R x\_\allowbreak{}1\$. Their average is\newline{}\$\textbackslash{}beta\textbackslash{}|x\textbackslash{}|\textasciicircum{}2/\allowbreak{}2\textbackslash{}mp\textbackslash{}beta Rx\_\allowbreak{}1\$,\allowbreak{} with minimizer distance \$R\$. Until \$J\$ is queried,\allowbreak{} its sign is hidden. A budget much smaller than \$n\$ misses it with constant probability,\allowbreak{} giving loss of order \$\textbackslash{}beta R\textasciicircum{}2\$. This construction requires a model allowing the component linear offsets.\newline{}\newline{}For an expected-budget lower-bound conversion,\allowbreak{} truncate after a sufficiently large constant multiple of the expected budget. Markov's inequality makes truncation unlikely enough to preserve a constant-probability hard-instance lower bound. This does not convert an expected-budget upper bound to a pathwise budget.\newline{}\newline{}Replicating the same hard function in every component preserves its one-function lower bound without multiplying by \$n\$. This covers nonsmooth strongly convex and one-dimensional logarithmic subclasses.\newline{}\newline{}In the cited span-restricted construction,\allowbreak{} individual smoothness is \$\textbackslash{}sqrt n\$ times the native mean-square parameter. Substitute native parameter \$\textbackslash{}beta/\allowbreak{}\textbackslash{}sqrt n\$ to obtain the recorded individual-smoothness lower bound. Keep the original span,\allowbreak{} dimension,\allowbreak{} and accuracy restrictions. Rescaling does not expand the lower algorithm class.\par\endgroup

\begingroup\raggedright\sloppy If a global minimizer lies within distance \$R\$ of \$x\_\allowbreak{}0\$,\allowbreak{} query on \$B(x\_\allowbreak{}0,\allowbreak{}R)\$. Since \$\textbackslash{}nabla f(x\textasciicircum{}\textbackslash{}star)=\allowbreak{}0\$,\allowbreak{} gradients there have norm at most \$2\textbackslash{}beta R\$. The centroid certificate gives \$O(d\textbackslash{}log(2+\textbackslash{}beta R\textasciicircum{}2/\allowbreak{}\textbackslash{}epsilon))\$ gradient calls. Smoothness gives \$f(x\_\allowbreak{}0)-f\textasciicircum{}\textbackslash{}star\textbackslash{}le\textbackslash{}beta R\textasciicircum{}2/\allowbreak{}2\$,\allowbreak{} including the zero-query endpoint.\newline{}\newline{}With global \$\textbackslash{}mu\$-strong convexity and initial gap \$\textbackslash{}Delta\$,\allowbreak{} use radius \$\textbackslash{}sqrt\{2\textbackslash{}Delta/\allowbreak{}\textbackslash{}mu\}\$,\allowbreak{} obtaining \$O(d\textbackslash{}log(2+\textbackslash{}kappa\textbackslash{}Delta/\allowbreak{}\textbackslash{}epsilon))\$. At \$\textbackslash{}mu=\allowbreak{}\textbackslash{}beta\$,\allowbreak{} equality in strong monotonicity and Lipschitz continuity forces \$\textbackslash{}nabla f(x)-\textbackslash{}nabla f(y)=\allowbreak{}\textbackslash{}beta(x-y)\$. One gradient identifies the minimizer of this known-curvature quadratic plus unknown affine term. Opposite translations exclude zero calls at nontrivial accuracy.\newline{}\newline{}Under global H{\AtlasUnicodeText ö}\allowbreak{}lder smoothness in \$\textbackslash{}ell\_\allowbreak{}q\$,\allowbreak{} convert to Euclidean quantities\newline{}\$\textbackslash{}beta\_\allowbreak{}E=\allowbreak{}\textbackslash{}beta\_\allowbreak{}\textbackslash{}nu d\textasciicircum{}\{(1+\textbackslash{}nu)(1/\allowbreak{}q-1/\allowbreak{}2)\_\allowbreak{}+\}\$ and\newline{}\$R\_\allowbreak{}E=\allowbreak{}Rd\textasciicircum{}\{(1/\allowbreak{}2-1/\allowbreak{}p)\_\allowbreak{}+\}\$. Gradients on the localization ball are at most \$\textbackslash{}beta\_\allowbreak{}E(2R\_\allowbreak{}E)\textasciicircum{}\textbackslash{}nu\$,\allowbreak{} giving\newline{}\$C\_\allowbreak{}\textbackslash{}nu d\textbackslash{}log(2+\textbackslash{}beta\_\allowbreak{}E R\_\allowbreak{}E\textasciicircum{}\{1+\textbackslash{}nu\}/\allowbreak{}\textbackslash{}epsilon)\$.\newline{}A boundary minimizer of an arbitrary constrained problem does not justify the zero-gradient premise. With two public norm-distance bounds,\allowbreak{} their intersection lies in the Euclidean ball of radius \$R\_\allowbreak{}\{2,\allowbreak{}+\}\$,\allowbreak{} while the Euclidean ball of radius \$R\_\allowbreak{}\{2,\allowbreak{}-\}\$ satisfies both promises. The former gives a certificate upper bound;\allowbreak{} embedding the one-dimensional hard family in the latter gives the logarithmic lower bound.\newline{}\newline{}For gradient-norm accuracy,\allowbreak{} use \$\textbackslash{}|\textbackslash{}nabla f(x)\textbackslash{}|\textasciicircum{}2\textbackslash{}le2\textbackslash{}beta(f(x)-f\textasciicircum{}\textbackslash{}star)\$. Under initial distance,\allowbreak{} target gap \$\textbackslash{}epsilon\textasciicircum{}2/\allowbreak{}(2\textbackslash{}beta)\$. Under initial gap alone,\allowbreak{} instead set\newline{}\$\$\newline{}F\_\allowbreak{}\textbackslash{}lambda=\allowbreak{}f+\textbackslash{}lambda\textbackslash{}|x-x\_\allowbreak{}0\textbackslash{}|\textasciicircum{}2/\allowbreak{}2,\allowbreak{}\textbackslash{}qquad\textbackslash{}lambda=\allowbreak{}\textbackslash{}epsilon\textasciicircum{}2/\allowbreak{}(32\textbackslash{}Delta).\newline{}\$\$\newline{}Its minimizer lies within \$8\textbackslash{}Delta/\allowbreak{}\textbackslash{}epsilon\$. A certificate at gap \$\textbackslash{}epsilon\textasciicircum{}2/\allowbreak{}(128\textbackslash{}beta)\$ gives \$\textbackslash{}|\textbackslash{}nabla F\_\allowbreak{}\textbackslash{}lambda(\textbackslash{}widehat x)\textbackslash{}|\textbackslash{}le\textbackslash{}epsilon/\allowbreak{}4\$,\allowbreak{} while the public regularizer contributes at most \$\textbackslash{}epsilon/\allowbreak{}4\$. Each regularized gradient costs one original gradient,\allowbreak{} and the budget is \$O(d\textbackslash{}log(2+\textbackslash{}beta\textbackslash{}Delta/\allowbreak{}\textbackslash{}epsilon\textasciicircum{}2))\$.\newline{}\newline{}For lower transfers,\allowbreak{} strong convexity gives \$f-f\textasciicircum{}\textbackslash{}star\textbackslash{}le\textbackslash{}|\textbackslash{}nabla f\textbackslash{}|\textasciicircum{}2/\allowbreak{}(2\textbackslash{}mu)\$. Choose the hard subclass modulus proportional to \$\textbackslash{}epsilon/\allowbreak{}R\$,\allowbreak{} or \$\textbackslash{}epsilon\textasciicircum{}2/\allowbreak{}\textbackslash{}Delta\$,\allowbreak{} for the two respective initializations. Gradient accuracy forces constant relative gap reduction. Apply the cited deterministic chain or randomized matrix-query theorem in its original dimension window;\allowbreak{} truncate only to constructions that fit. This preserves initialization,\allowbreak{} guarantee,\allowbreak{} and algorithm scope.\newline{}\newline{}For an already strongly convex model,\allowbreak{} the gap threshold required for the lower transfer is \$\textbackslash{}epsilon\textasciicircum{}2/\allowbreak{}(2\textbackslash{}mu)\$,\allowbreak{} whereas the sufficient gap for the upper transfer is \$\textbackslash{}epsilon\textasciicircum{}2/\allowbreak{}(2\textbackslash{}beta)\$. Retain these different logarithm arguments rather than silently canceling their condition-number shift. For \$1<\textbackslash{}kappa\textbackslash{}le4\$,\allowbreak{} gradient descent and the nested one-dimensional construction yield the stated comparable near-unit denominators. At \$\textbackslash{}kappa=\allowbreak{}1\$,\allowbreak{} the known-curvature quadratic is solved in one call.\newline{}\newline{}For matching \$\textbackslash{}ell\_\allowbreak{}p\$ H{\AtlasUnicodeText ö}\allowbreak{}lder geometry,\allowbreak{} the descent model along a dual steepest-descent direction gives\newline{}\$f(x)-f\textasciicircum{}\textbackslash{}star\textbackslash{}ge c\_\allowbreak{}\textbackslash{}nu\textbackslash{}beta\_\allowbreak{}\textbackslash{}nu\textasciicircum{}\{-1/\allowbreak{}\textbackslash{}nu\}\textbackslash{}|\textbackslash{}nabla f(x)\textbackslash{}|\_\allowbreak{}\{p\textasciicircum{}\textbackslash{}star\}\textasciicircum{}\{(1+\textbackslash{}nu)/\allowbreak{}\textbackslash{}nu\}\$.\newline{}Targeting gap \$c\_\allowbreak{}\textbackslash{}nu\textbackslash{}beta\_\allowbreak{}\textbackslash{}nu\textasciicircum{}\{-1/\allowbreak{}\textbackslash{}nu\}\textbackslash{}epsilon\textasciicircum{}\{(1+\textbackslash{}nu)/\allowbreak{}\textbackslash{}nu\}\$ in the localization certificate therefore gives\newline{}\$C\_\allowbreak{}\textbackslash{}nu d\textbackslash{}log(2+\textbackslash{}beta\_\allowbreak{}\textbackslash{}nu R\textasciicircum{}\textbackslash{}nu/\allowbreak{}\textbackslash{}epsilon)\$.\par\endgroup

\begingroup\raggedright\sloppy Let \$Q\textbackslash{}subset\textbackslash{}mathbb R\textasciicircum{}d\$ be public,\allowbreak{} compact,\allowbreak{} convex,\allowbreak{} and full dimensional,\allowbreak{} with diameter at most \$D\$ in the stated norm. Suppose all returned subgradients have dual norm at most \$L\$. Query \$g\_\allowbreak{}i\textbackslash{}in\textbackslash{}partial f(x\_\allowbreak{}i)\$ at the centroid of the current body and retain \$\textbackslash{}langle g\_\allowbreak{}i,\allowbreak{}x\_\allowbreak{}i-x\textbackslash{}rangle\textbackslash{}ge0\$. The centroid halfspace theorem bounds the retained volume by \$(1-e\textasciicircum{}\{-1\})\textasciicircum{}T\textbackslash{}operatorname\{vol\}(Q)\$.\newline{}\newline{}The computable certificate is\newline{}\$\$\newline{}\textbackslash{}Gamma\_\allowbreak{}T=\allowbreak{}\textbackslash{}min\_\allowbreak{}\{\textbackslash{}lambda\textbackslash{}in\textbackslash{}Delta\_\allowbreak{}T\}\textbackslash{}max\_\allowbreak{}\{x\textbackslash{}in Q\}\textbackslash{}sum\_\allowbreak{}i\textbackslash{}lambda\_\allowbreak{}i\textbackslash{}langle g\_\allowbreak{}i,\allowbreak{}x\_\allowbreak{}i-x\textbackslash{}rangle\newline{}=\allowbreak{}\textbackslash{}max\_\allowbreak{}\{x\textbackslash{}in Q\}\textbackslash{}min\_\allowbreak{}i\textbackslash{}langle g\_\allowbreak{}i,\allowbreak{}x\_\allowbreak{}i-x\textbackslash{}rangle.\newline{}\$\$\newline{}The equality is convex minimax. Subgradient inequalities and convexity imply\newline{}\$f(\textbackslash{}sum\_\allowbreak{}i\textbackslash{}lambda\_\allowbreak{}ix\_\allowbreak{}i)-\textbackslash{}min\_\allowbreak{}Qf\textbackslash{}le\textbackslash{}Gamma\_\allowbreak{}T\$.\newline{}If \$\textbackslash{}Gamma\_\allowbreak{}T>\textbackslash{}epsilon\$,\allowbreak{} choose \$z\textbackslash{}in Q\$ with all cut margins greater than \$\textbackslash{}epsilon\$. The copy \$(1-a)z+aQ\$,\allowbreak{} where \$a=\allowbreak{}\textbackslash{}epsilon/\allowbreak{}[2(\textbackslash{}epsilon+LD)]\$,\allowbreak{} survives every cut. Its volume is \$a\textasciicircum{}d\textbackslash{}operatorname\{vol\}(Q)\$,\allowbreak{} contradicting centroid shrinkage once \$T>C d\textbackslash{}log(2+LD/\allowbreak{}\textbackslash{}epsilon)\$. If the body loses volume earlier,\allowbreak{} the same positive-volume argument already certifies the error. No function values or inscribed-ball estimate are required.\newline{}\newline{}For \$Q=\allowbreak{}RB\_\allowbreak{}p\textasciicircum{}d\$ and \$\textbackslash{}ell\_\allowbreak{}q\$-Lipschitz objectives,\allowbreak{} use \$D=\allowbreak{}2Rd\textasciicircum{}\{(1/\allowbreak{}q-1/\allowbreak{}p)\_\allowbreak{}+\}\$. Returning the center has error at most \$LRd\textasciicircum{}\{(1/\allowbreak{}q-1/\allowbreak{}p)\_\allowbreak{}+\}\$,\allowbreak{} giving the coarse zero-query regime. Exact centroid,\allowbreak{} minimax,\allowbreak{} and public geometric calculations are uncharged internal operations.\newline{}\newline{}For a deterministic selector with total movement at most \$W(T)\$ on nested convex sets,\allowbreak{} instead impose deep cuts of margin \$2LW(T)/\allowbreak{}T\$. If all \$T\$ sets are nonempty,\allowbreak{} every move has length at least \$2W(T)/\allowbreak{}T\$,\allowbreak{} contradicting the movement bound. At the first empty intersection,\allowbreak{} minimax gives error at most \$2LW(T)/\allowbreak{}T\$. Substitution of the cited stable-movement theorem yields the recorded nondual upper bound. Its deterministic information scope is distinct from the scope of randomized implementations.\par\endgroup

Strong convexity gives F(y)>=\allowbreak{}F(x)+<grad F(x),\allowbreak{}y-x>+mu||y-x||\textasciicircum{}2/\allowbreak{}2. Taking the infimum in y yields ||grad F(x)||\textasciicircum{}2>=\allowbreak{}2mu(F(x)-F*),\allowbreak{} so the source PL assumption follows without any assumption on component convexity. Set L\_\allowbreak{}ms=\allowbreak{}beta and kappa\_\allowbreak{}ms=\allowbreak{}beta/\allowbreak{}mu. Algorithm 1 computes only gradients:\allowbreak{} an initial/\allowbreak{}refresh mean costs n calls;\allowbreak{} a sampled difference costs two calls. With p\_\allowbreak{}refresh=\allowbreak{}1/\allowbreak{}(n+1),\allowbreak{} its expected update cost is p\_\allowbreak{}refresh*n+2(1-p\_\allowbreak{}refresh)<=\allowbreak{}3. Put A=\allowbreak{}kappa(1+sqrt(n)),\allowbreak{} T=\allowbreak{}ceil(4(n+A)),\allowbreak{} q=\allowbreak{}A/\allowbreak{}T<=\allowbreak{}1/\allowbreak{}4,\allowbreak{} and s=\allowbreak{}ceil(log(Delta/\allowbreak{}epsilon)/\allowbreak{}log(1/\allowbreak{}q)). Lemma E.1 bounds conditional expected epoch gap by q times the input gap,\allowbreak{} and cost by n+3T. Tower expectation gives expected output gap <=\allowbreak{}q\textasciicircum{}s Delta<=\allowbreak{}epsilon and expected calls <=\allowbreak{}s(n+3T). For 1<=\allowbreak{}kappa<=\allowbreak{}sqrt(n),\allowbreak{} T=\allowbreak{}Theta(n),\allowbreak{} log(1/\allowbreak{}q)=\allowbreak{}Theta(1+log(sqrt(n)/\allowbreak{}kappa)),\allowbreak{} uniformly also at n=\allowbreak{}1. Thus cost is O(n+n log(Delta/\allowbreak{}epsilon)/\allowbreak{}(1+log(sqrt(n)/\allowbreak{}kappa))). No source function values,\allowbreak{} unknown F*,\allowbreak{} extra certificate,\allowbreak{} distance bound or prescribed high dimension are used.\par\endgroup

\begingroup\raggedright\sloppy Retain the frozen FO\_\allowbreak{}FINITE\_\allowbreak{}SUM\_\allowbreak{}SIMULATION and FO\_\allowbreak{}SMOOTH\_\allowbreak{}LOCALIZATION premises,\allowbreak{} not their unrelated external theorems. Mean-square component smoothness implies ||grad F(x)-grad F(y)||<=\allowbreak{}beta||x-y|| by Jensen. At beta=\allowbreak{}mu,\allowbreak{} for v=\allowbreak{}x-y,\allowbreak{} strong monotonicity and Cauchy-Schwarz give mu||v||\textasciicircum{}2<=\allowbreak{}<grad F(x)-grad F(y),\allowbreak{}v><=\allowbreak{}||grad F(x)-grad F(y)|| ||v||<=\allowbreak{}mu||v||\textasciicircum{}2. Equality forces grad F(x)-grad F(y)=\allowbreak{}mu(x-y). Query all n components at the public initial point x0,\allowbreak{} form g=\allowbreak{}grad F(x0),\allowbreak{} and return x0-g/\allowbreak{}mu. Its gradient is zero,\allowbreak{} so its loss is exactly zero;\allowbreak{} total component cost is exactly n for every d and epsilon in the unchanged contract. This is an upper cost,\allowbreak{} not an assertion that expected-cost minimax complexity equals n. No R promise is used. Zero cost cannot meet epsilon<Delta uniformly:\allowbreak{} at x0=\allowbreak{}0 take all components equal to mu||x-s a e1||\textasciicircum{}2/\allowbreak{}2 with s in \{+1,\allowbreak{}-1\} and a=\allowbreak{}sqrt(2Delta/\allowbreak{}mu). These instances meet mean-square beta-smoothness for every beta>=\allowbreak{}mu and have initial gap Delta. The average loss of any zero-information output X over the two signs is Delta+mu E||X||\textasciicircum{}2/\allowbreak{}2>=\allowbreak{}Delta. Separately retain bound b5 at its exact frozen statement:\allowbreak{} its native view,\allowbreak{} g1,\allowbreak{} q1 and resource projection equal those of randomized comparison c1,\allowbreak{} and region r3 is a subset of r2 by its predicate. Hence b5 can be referenced in c1 only with guard r3. This does not extend b5 to any new parameters or certify its old source again. The same n-call algorithm satisfies the deterministic view pointwise on every path;\allowbreak{} record it separately as deterministic b3 with its own q1 and unit-condition region. No scientific quantity IDs are merged.\par\endgroup
